emergency.note: Unified 911 covers Riyadh; legacy numbers 999 (police) and 997 (ambulance) still work, and English-speaking operators are generally available.

avoid.reason: Crime is very low; the real cautions are aggressive driving and strict local laws — avoid photographing government buildings or people without permission.

hood_desc: Riyadh's modern commercial heart along Olaya and Tahlia streets, with skyscrapers like the Kingdom Centre, hotels, malls and restaurants; suits business travelers and first-timers wanting central buzz.
An older, established central district on the original grid, with government offices, stadiums and affordable dining; suits budget travelers and those wanting an authentic, less glossy Riyadh.
A gated, leafy enclave of embassies west of the center, green, secure and low-rise; suits diplomats and those seeking calm, upscale, walkable surroundings.
An affluent modern northern residential district near business hubs, with villas and malls; suits families and long-stay visitors wanting newer, upscale housing.
A gleaming new business megaproject of towers and skybridges in the north with its own metro station; suits business visitors and those wanting cutting-edge modern surroundings.

water.note: Treated water meets standards, but bottled water is recommended, especially outside modern hotels.

transit.pay: Use the rechargeable Darb card, tapped at turnstiles for both Metro and Riyadh Bus; buy/load it at station vending machines or the Darb app (contactless bank cards are not yet accepted for entry). Flat fare is about SAR 4 (~$1.07) per trip, with free transfers within a set window.
transit.hours: Metro and buses run roughly 5:30am-midnight Saturday-Wednesday, later on Thursday, and from early afternoon on Friday; there is no overnight service.

landmarks: Kingdom Centre Tower
A sleek 302m skyscraper with a distinctive inverted-parabola opening and glass Sky Bridge offering panoramic city views, making it Riyadh's most photographed skyline icon.
Al Faisaliah Tower
One of Saudi Arabia's first skyscrapers, its golden glass sphere near the top makes it instantly recognizable against the desert sky.
Al Masmak Palace (Masmak Fortress)
A 19th-century clay-and-mudbrick fort central to the founding of modern Saudi Arabia, prized for its atmospheric thick walls and iconic wooden door.
At-Turaif District, Diriyah
A UNESCO World Heritage mudbrick citadel and birthplace of the first Saudi state, striking for its traditional Najdi architecture at golden hour.
National Museum of Saudi Arabia
A modern museum with bold architectural forms that traces the country's history, popular for its striking exterior design.
Murabba Palace
A historic mudbrick royal palace built by King Abdulaziz, valued for its authentic early-20th-century Najdi architectural detail.
King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD)
A futuristic business district of striking modern towers, including the lattice-clad Conference Center, that has become a new symbol of Riyadh's skyline.
Wadi Hanifa
A restored green valley winding through the city, offering a rare lush, water-filled landscape contrast to Riyadh's desert setting.
Al Bujairi Heritage Park
A restored heritage district overlooking At-Turaif in Diriyah, known for illuminated evening views of the old city across the valley.
Riyadh Zoo
A 55-acre public zoo in Al Malaz with more than a thousand animals, a miniature train circling the grounds, and free admission for visitors.

train.note: Riyadh has domestic trains only. SAR runs frequent Riyadh-Dammam services and the 'North Train' from Riyadh (King Khalid Intl Airport station) to Qassim, Hail and Al Jouf/Qurayyat, including overnight sleeper trains with private berths. No international rail yet - the GCC cross-border line is still under construction.

bus.note: SAPTCO runs international coaches from Riyadh's main bus terminal to Gulf and Arab neighbours (UAE and Bahrain, plus onward connections). Carry your passport and any required visas for cross-border trips.

ferry.note: Riyadh sits in central Arabia with no coastline, so there are no ferries. The nearest sea crossings leave from Jeddah (Red Sea) or Dammam (Arabian Gulf).
